brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: Which two axes form the foundation of the Social Style Selling framework?
choices: Introversion vs. Extraversion, and Thinking vs. Feeling
Task vs. People, and Ask vs. Tell
Speed vs. Accuracy, and Logic vs. Emotion
Relationships vs. Results, and Direct vs. Indirect
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the two-axis framework is built on Task vs. People (what drives behavior) and Ask vs. Tell (how someone gets what they want).
questions.feedback_incorrect: The model is not based on personality tests or psychology labels. The two axes are Task vs. People and Ask vs. Tell, which describe observable communication behavior.

questions.question: What is the signature question a Driver tends to lead with?
choices: How does this work and how was it measured?
Who else is using this and who should be involved?
What are the results and what is the outcome?
Why this solution and why should we trust you?
questions.feedback_correct: Right—Drivers ask "What?" because they are focused on results and outcomes, not process or relationships.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Drivers are task-focused and results-oriented, so their signature question centers on outcomes and speed. "How?" is Analytical, "Who?" is Expressive, and "Why?" is Amiable.

questions.question: How does an Analytical typically behave under pressure in a sales conversation?
choices: Takes control of the meeting and directs the conversation
Asks for more time and requests additional data
Becomes argumentative and pushes back hard
Goes quiet, withdraws, and avoids engagement
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—when pressured, Analyticals pull back and seek more information, data, and time to evaluate because they need to feel confident in their decision.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Pressure behaviors are specific to each style. Analyticals respond to pressure by asking for more data and time, not by taking control (Driver), arguing (Expressive), or withdrawing (Amiable).

questions.question: What is the primary difference between an Expressive and an Amiable, given that both are high-emotion styles?
choices: Expressives are focused on tasks while Amiables are focused on people
Expressives tell and hold the floor; Amiables ask and draw others out
Expressives are warm and soft-spoken; Amiables are animated and storytelling
Expressives avoid conflict while Amiables seek recognition and visibility
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—both are high-emotion, but the key separator is the X axis: Expressives tell and dominate the conversation, while Amiables ask and invite input.
questions.feedback_incorrect: While both Expressives and Amiables show emotion openly, what separates them is their communication style on the Ask vs. Tell axis. Expressives tell stories and hold the floor; Amiables ask questions and draw you out.

questions.question: When preparing to sell to an Analytical buyer, what should you prioritize?
choices: Building rapport and emphasizing the relationship and trust
Sharing your vision and getting their buy-in on big possibilities
Preparing detailed, logical questions and using evidence throughout
Minimizing detail and keeping the energy high and conversational
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—Analyticals need rigor and proof, so detailed questions and evidence-based reasoning are essential to earning their confidence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Analyticals are task-focused and methodical. They need to see the logic and data behind your approach, not rapport-building, vision, or high energy.

questions.question: What does it mean when the instructor notes state that "style describes observable behavior only"?
choices: Style is a permanent personality trait that never changes
Style is based on how someone communicates right now, not their entire character or worth
Style can only be measured through formal personality assessments
Style determines someone's intelligence and ability to succeed
questions.feedback_correct: Right—style is about what you can observe in how someone communicates, not a judgment about who they are as a person.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The model is built on observable behavior—how someone asks questions, shows emotion, and focuses attention. It does not define someone's intelligence, worth, or potential.

questions.question: Your own Social Style has an impact on how you sell—what is the core challenge this creates?
choices: Your natural selling approach may land poorly on buyers with a different style, creating unintended friction
You should change your personality completely to match each buyer type
Buyers with your same style will always trust you more than buyers with different styles
Your Social Style determines which product categories you can sell most effectively
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—a Driver rep's direct, results-focused approach may shut down an Amiable before the conversation starts, even though it works perfectly with other Drivers.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The point is not to change who you are, but to recognize that your natural style lands differently depending on the buyer. A Driver's directness that energizes one buyer may stress another.

questions.question: When you notice a buyer showing a pressure behavior mid-meeting, what does that signal tell you about what has happened?
choices: The buyer is not interested and you should end the meeting immediately
Something has broken down in the conversation—it is an early warning sign to slow down and shift your approach
The buyer's Social Style has changed and you need to start the discovery process over
You have chosen the wrong product and should suggest an alternative immediately
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—a pressure behavior is not a personality flaw; it is a signal that your approach is not landing and you have a chance to recover before trust is damaged.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Pressure behaviors (Driver taking control, Analytical requesting time, Expressive arguing, Amiable withdrawing) are signals that something is off in your communication approach, not that the relationship is over.

questions.question: How should you adjust your selling approach when a buyer has an adjacent style mixed with their primary style?
choices: Treat them as two separate buyers and alternate your approach every few minutes
Ignore the adjacent style and focus only on the primary style behaviors
Recognize that the adjacent style softens or modifies the primary style, so expect mixed signals and adjust accordingly
Ask the buyer directly which style they prefer so you know exactly how to communicate
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—an Analytical with an Amiable adjacent will still be methodical but more relationship-conscious, so recognizing that blend helps you avoid confusion.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Adjacent styles exist in the quadrant next to the primary style and they modify how the primary style shows up in behavior. A Driver with Expressive adjacent will be warmer than a pure Driver, for example.

questions.question: Based on the course, what is the single disciplined habit that defines versatility in Social Style Selling?
choices: Developing four different personas so you can be anyone to anyone
Learning to recognize when you naturally match a buyer's style and leaning into that advantage
Read the cues, name the style, and adjust your approach accordingly
Practicing each style equally so you never favor one over the others
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—versatility is not about becoming someone else; it is the deliberate, repeatable habit of observing, naming, and adapting.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Versatility is a skill built through one disciplined habit: reading observable cues, identifying the style, and consciously adjusting your communication approach to reduce friction and increase connection.
